title: Bengaluru's Legendary MTR Is Opening in Sydney, Bringing Its Century-Old Dosas to Australia
excerpt: Australia's assistant minister for multicultural affairs confirmed the 102-year-old Mavalli Tiffin Rooms will franchise in Sydney, adding to a growing list of international outposts.
body:
• Mavalli Tiffin Rooms (MTR), the 102-year-old Bengaluru restaurant credited with inventing the rava idli, is opening a franchise in Sydney, Australia.
  • The announcement was made by Julian Hill, Australia's Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs, after visiting the original restaurant in Bengaluru.
  • MTR already operates in Singapore, Dubai, Kuala Lumpur, Bangkok, Seattle, Toronto, Bristol, and other international cities.
  • The restaurant has been owned and run by the Maiya family since its founding in 1924.

Mavalli Tiffin Rooms, the Bengaluru institution that has served filter coffee and crisp dosas from the same Lalbagh Road address for more than a century, is heading to Australia. The restaurant will open a franchise location in Sydney, adding to a growing international network that already spans eight countries.

The news came from an unlikely source: Julian Hill, Australia's Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs, who posted about the expansion on Instagram after visiting the original MTR location in Bengaluru. "MTR is coming to Australia! Bengaluru's iconic heritage restaurant, over 100 years old, Mavalli Tiffin Rooms is franchising in Sydney. Literally the best dosa ever," Hill wrote alongside photos of himself eating dosa, vada, and filter coffee.

A Restaurant That Invented a Dish

MTR's story begins in 1924, when brothers Ganappaiah Maiya and Parameshwara Maiya opened a small eatery called Brahmins' Coffee Club on Lalbagh Fort Road in Bengaluru. After Parameshwara's death in 1933, their brother Yagnanarayana Maiya took over and renamed the establishment Mavalli Tiffin Rooms.

The restaurant's most enduring contribution to Indian cuisine came during the Second World War. When rice became scarce due to wartime shortages, Yagnanarayana Maiya experimented with semolina and sour curd, steaming the batter instead of using the traditional rice-based preparation. The result was the rava idli, now one of the most popular breakfast items across South India.

"Literally the best dosa ever."

— Julian Hill, Australia's Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs

In 1959, MTR moved to its current Art Deco building on Lalbagh Road and introduced an open kitchen concept, allowing customers to walk through and watch their food being prepared — an unusual practice at the time.

A Growing International Footprint

Today, MTR is run by the third generation of the Maiya family, including Hemamalini Maiya, Vikram Maiya, and Arvind Maiya. Under their oversight, the restaurant has expanded beyond its Bengaluru home base to other Indian cities and a string of international locations including Singapore, Dubai, Kuala Lumpur, Bangkok, Seattle, Toronto, and Bristol.

The expansion outside the original location began in 2004 with additional branches in Karnataka, followed by overseas openings in subsequent years. Each location has attempted to replicate the core menu — dosas, idlis, vadas, and filter coffee — that made the original famous.

What It Means for Australia's Indian Community

Australia is home to one of the fastest-growing Indian diaspora communities in the world. According to the 2021 census, people of Indian ancestry constituted the second-largest group of overseas-born residents in Australia, with particularly large communities in Sydney and Melbourne.

For many in that community, MTR represents more than a restaurant chain. It is a specific taste memory — the kind of institution whose name evokes family trips to Bengaluru, early morning queues on Lalbagh Road, and the particular crispness of a dosa made the way their grandparents ordered it.

Sydney's franchise will test whether that nostalgia, combined with MTR's reputation, can compete in a city already well-served by South Indian restaurants. If the other international locations are any guide, the answer is probably yes — but the rava idli will have to speak for itself.
